blocks.content: The Banker's Algorithm is the landmark formal method for deadlock avoidance, developed by Edsger Dijkstra. Instead of forbidding entire categories of behavior the way deadlock prevention does, it looks at the exact state of the system at this instant and grants a resource request only when doing so is guaranteed to leave every process with some path to eventually finish.

This chapter builds the algorithm from the ground up around one concrete, consistent example that runs through the whole discussion: five processes and three resource types with real numbers in every matrix. You will see the analogy the algorithm is named after, the exact data it needs, the Need matrix computed by hand, the Safety Algorithm traced to a genuine safe sequence, the Resource Request Algorithm evaluated against a real request, and why, despite being one of the most famous results in operating systems, production kernels almost never use it as written.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785408758469-167756344.png
1. The Banker's Analogy

Picture a small town bank with a fixed pool of cash sitting in its vault. A handful of customers each carry a maximum credit line, the largest amount they are permitted to borrow in total. When a customer asks for money, the banker does not simply check whether enough cash is physically sitting in the vault right now. Before saying yes, the banker mentally works through a harder question: if this loan is handed out, is there still some order in which every current customer could eventually receive their full maximum credit line and pay it back?

If the answer is yes, the loan is safe to approve immediately. If there is even a chance that granting this particular loan could leave the bank in a corner where no arrangement lets every customer eventually be paid in full, the banker refuses or delays the request, even though the cash is sitting right there and could technically be handed over this second.

The operating system plays the exact same role. Cash in the vault becomes the Available vector, a customer's maximum credit line becomes a process's declared Max, money already lent out becomes the Allocation already held by a process, and the banker's mental check before approving becomes the Safety Algorithm the OS runs before granting any request. The promise in both worlds is identical: never make a commitment that could later trap you with no safe way out, even when the resources appear to be sitting there idle.
A request is granted only if, after granting it, the system is still guaranteed to have some order in which every process can finish. Being technically available right now is not, by itself, enough.

blocks.title: Available does not mean grantable
blocks.content: The single hardest idea to internalize about this algorithm is that having enough free resources on hand does not automatically mean a request should be granted. The algorithm can, and routinely does, refuse a request it could physically satisfy this instant, purely because granting it would remove the guarantee that every process can still finish.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785408758469-58016766.png
2. The Data the Algorithm Needs

The algorithm operates on four pieces of data for a system of n processes and m resource types. Three of them are tracked directly, and the fourth is always computed live from the other two rather than stored on its own.

["Allocation: an n by m matrix where row i gives how many instances of each resource type process Pi currently holds.","Max: an n by m matrix where row i gives the maximum number of instances of each resource type Pi may ever request over its entire lifetime, declared up front when the process starts.","Available: a vector of length m giving how many instances of each resource type are currently free and unallocated to any process.","Need: an n by m matrix, derived rather than declared, where Need of Pi for resource type j equals Max of Pi for that type minus Allocation of Pi for that type."]
items: Allocation: an n by m matrix where row i gives how many instances of each resource type process Pi currently holds.
Max: an n by m matrix where row i gives the maximum number of instances of each resource type Pi may ever request over its entire lifetime, declared up front when the process starts.
Available: a vector of length m giving how many instances of each resource type are currently free and unallocated to any process.
Need: an n by m matrix, derived rather than declared, where Need of Pi for resource type j equals Max of Pi for that type minus Allocation of Pi for that type.

blocks.content: Max is the strong, somewhat unrealistic assumption the whole algorithm rests on: every process must state its worst case future demand before it ever runs, and it may never exceed that ceiling later. Allocation and Available are dynamic and change constantly as processes acquire and release resources while the system runs, while Max stays fixed for a process's entire lifetime once declared. Need is simply a live view recomputed from Max and Allocation whenever it is needed, never stored as an independent source of truth.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785408758469-66532637.png
3. A Concrete Scenario: Five Processes, Three Resource Types
blocks.text: 3. A Concrete Scenario: Five Processes, Three Resource Types

blocks.content: To make every later step concrete, this chapter uses one running scenario throughout. There are five processes, P0 through P4, and three resource types, A, B and C, with total instances in the system of A equal to 10, B equal to 5, and C equal to 7. At the moment we start our trace, the processes already hold some resources, recorded in the Allocation matrix below.
Each process also declared its own maximum possible demand when it started, recorded in the Max matrix below. This is the ceiling each process promised never to cross.

Available is found by taking the total instances of each resource type and subtracting how many are currently allocated across every process. Summing the Allocation column for A gives 0 plus 2 plus 3 plus 2 plus 0, which is 7, so Available for A is 10 minus 7, which is 3. The same arithmetic for B and C gives the full Available vector shown below.

blocks.alt: A Concrete Scenario: Five Processes, Three Resource Types

blocks.content: 4. The Need Matrix

Need for process Pi and resource type j is defined as Max of Pi for j minus Allocation of Pi for j. It answers a very specific question: given what a process already holds, how many more instances of each resource type could it still possibly ask for before hitting the ceiling it declared. Take P0 as a worked example: its Max row is 7, 5, 3 and its Allocation row is 0, 1, 0, so its Need row is 7 minus 0, 5 minus 1, and 3 minus 0, which comes out to 7, 4, 3.

Applying the same subtraction to every row of the scenario from Section 3 produces the full Need matrix below. This table is the single most important derived value in the whole algorithm, since both the Safety Algorithm and the Resource Request Algorithm are built directly on top of it.

blocks.title: A quick sanity check
blocks.content: For every single row, Need plus Allocation must equal Max exactly, with no exceptions. Check P1: its Need is 1, 2, 2 and its Allocation is 2, 0, 0, and adding them gives 3, 2, 2, which is exactly its declared Max. If this check ever fails for any row, the Need matrix was computed incorrectly.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785408759062-83878914.png
5. The Safety Algorithm, Step by Step
blocks.text: 5. The Safety Algorithm, Step by Step

blocks.content: The Safety Algorithm decides whether a given state, meaning a specific Allocation, Need and Available, is safe. It begins by copying Available into a working vector called Work, and marking every process as unfinished by setting Finish of i to false for all i. It then repeatedly scans the unfinished processes looking for any single process i whose entire Need row fits inside Work, meaning every resource type in Need i is less than or equal to the matching entry in Work.

Whenever such a process is found, the algorithm pretends that process runs to completion right now. It marks Finish of i as true and adds the whole Allocation row of that process back into Work, modeling the assumption that once a process could obtain everything it might ever need, it will eventually finish its work and hand back every resource it was holding. The scan then restarts from the beginning, since a process that did not fit a moment ago might fit now that Work has grown.

This repeats until one of two things happens. If a complete scan finds no unfinished process whose Need fits inside the current Work, and at least one process still has Finish equal to false, the algorithm stops and declares the state unsafe, since no ordering exists that lets every process finish. If every process eventually reaches Finish equal to true, the state is safe, and the exact order in which processes were marked finished is a valid safe sequence. That order is not required to be unique; the algorithm only needs to find one.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785408759063-400105612.png
blocks.alt: The Safety Algorithm, Step by Step

blocks.content: 6. Worked Example: Finding a Safe Sequence
blocks.text: 6. Worked Example: Finding a Safe Sequence

blocks.content: Now the Safety Algorithm runs on the exact scenario built in Sections 3 and 4. Work starts as a copy of Available, which is 3, 3, 2, and every Finish flag starts false. P0 is checked first simply because it is listed first, but its Need of 7, 4, 3 does not fit inside 3, 3, 2 on the A dimension, so it is skipped for now. P1 is checked next, and its Need of 1, 2, 2 fits entirely inside 3, 3, 2, so P1 is chosen, and its Allocation of 2, 0, 0 is added back into Work.

The scan restarts and continues the same way: at each step, every remaining unfinished process is checked against the current Work, and whichever one fits is picked, with its Allocation released back into Work before the next round begins. The full trace is shown below.

Every process reaches Finish equal to true, so the state described in Section 3 is safe, and P1, P3, P4, P0, P2 is a valid safe sequence. Notice that the final Available after all five steps is 10, 5, 7, which exactly matches the total instances of each resource type from Section 3, confirming every unit that was ever allocated has been correctly accounted for and released.

blocks.title: A safe sequence is not unique
blocks.content: Nothing about the algorithm guarantees only one safe order exists; it only needs to find one to declare the state safe. In this trace, once P1 finishes, both P3 and P4 individually happen to fit against the new Work, and either could legally have been picked next. Safety is a statement about existence, at least one workable order, not about a single predetermined path.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785408759063-276295687.png
blocks.alt: Worked Example: Finding a Safe Sequence

blocks.content: 7. The Resource Request Algorithm, Step by Step
blocks.text: 7. The Resource Request Algorithm, Step by Step

blocks.content: The Safety Algorithm on its own only answers a yes or no question about a fixed state. The Resource Request Algorithm is what actually decides, live, whether to grant a real request from a process Pi for a vector of additional resource units, called Request i. It runs three checks in order, and the first two are simple bound checks that exist specifically to avoid running the expensive third check when it is obviously unnecessary.

["Check that Request i is within Need i for every resource type. If Pi is asking for more than it originally declared as its own maximum, this is a bug in the requesting process, and the request is rejected outright with no further work.","Check that Request i is within Available for every resource type. If the resources simply are not free right now, granting is impossible regardless of safety, so Pi must wait. This check alone filters out a large share of requests before the costly safety check ever needs to run.","If both checks pass, pretend to grant the request: subtract Request i from Available, add Request i to Allocation i, and subtract Request i from Need i, exactly as if the grant had actually happened. Then run the full Safety Algorithm from Section 5 on this hypothetical new state."]
items: Check that Request i is within Need i for every resource type. If Pi is asking for more than it originally declared as its own maximum, this is a bug in the requesting process, and the request is rejected outright with no further work.

Check that Request i is within Available for every resource type. If the resources simply are not free right now, granting is impossible regardless of safety, so Pi must wait. This check alone filters out a large share of requests before the costly safety check ever needs to run.

If both checks pass, pretend to grant the request: subtract Request i from Available, add Request i to Allocation i, and subtract Request i from Need i, exactly as if the grant had actually happened. Then run the full Safety Algorithm from Section 5 on this hypothetical new state.

blocks.content: If the hypothetical state that results is safe, the pretend grant becomes real: the updated Available, Allocation and Need are kept, and Pi proceeds immediately with its new resources. If the hypothetical state comes back unsafe, every one of those three updates is rolled back to exactly what it was before the pretend step, and Pi is made to wait, even though, a moment ago, the resources were technically sitting free.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785408759063-97349074.png
blocks.alt: The Resource Request Algorithm, Step by Step

blocks.content: 8. Worked Example: Evaluating a Resource Request
blocks.text: 8. Worked Example: Evaluating a Resource Request

blocks.content: Continue from the exact safe state built in Sections 3 and 4, before any process has actually finished. Suppose process P1 now issues a real request for one more instance of A, zero more of B, and two more instances of C, written as Request1 equal to 1, 0, 2. Check one asks whether this fits inside Need of P1, which is 1, 2, 2. Since 1 is at most 1, 0 is at most 2, and 2 is at most 2, the request fits and check one passes.

Check two asks whether the request fits inside the current Available, which is 3, 3, 2. Since 1, 0, 2 is at or under 3, 3, 2 on every entry, check two also passes, so the algorithm proceeds to pretend to grant. Available becomes 3, 3, 2 minus 1, 0, 2, which is 2, 3, 0. Allocation of P1 becomes 2, 0, 0 plus 1, 0, 2, which is 3, 0, 2. Need of P1 becomes 1, 2, 2 minus 1, 0, 2, which is 0, 2, 0. Every other process is untouched by this pretend update.

This hypothetical state is fed straight back into the Safety Algorithm, starting from the new Available of 2, 3, 0. P1 now fits first since its Need dropped to 0, 2, 0, releasing 3, 0, 2 back into Work. From there the trace runs P3, then P4, then P0, then P2, exactly as it did in Section 6, ending once again with every unit accounted for.

Since every process can still be finished in some order, the hypothetical state is safe, so the pretend grant is made real. P1 actually receives its extra 1, 0, 2 units, Available truly becomes 2, 3, 0, and P1 proceeds immediately with no waiting at all.

blocks.title: An instant rejection, no safety check needed
blocks.content: Suppose right after this grant, P0 asked for one more instance of C, a request of 0, 0, 1. Available for C is now 0, so check two fails immediately: the request exceeds what is currently free. The Safety Algorithm never even runs, and P0 simply waits until some other process finishes and releases a unit of C.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785408759064-72352803.png
blocks.alt: Worked Example: Evaluating a Resource Request

blocks.content: 9. Complexity, and Why Avoidance Is Rare in Production
blocks.text: 9. Complexity, and Why Avoidance Is Rare in Production

blocks.content: One full pass of the Safety Algorithm scans up to n processes, and for each unfinished process it compares an m length Need row against Work, which is an O of m comparison. In the worst case only one process becomes newly eligible per pass, exactly as happened in our own worked trace, so the algorithm can need up to n passes overall, giving a worst case cost proportional to n squared times m. With n equal to 5 and m equal to 3 in our own scenario that is a tiny amount of work, but the important detail is that this entire check must be repeated on every single resource request the system ever receives, not once at startup.

{"headers":["Approach","When the cost is paid","Rough cost per resource request"],"rows":[["Deadlock prevention","Once, baked into fixed design time rules such as a global lock ordering","Effectively no live check at request time"],["Deadlock avoidance, the Banker's method","On every single resource request, without exception","Proportional to processes squared times resource types, worst case"],["Deadlock detection and recovery","Only occasionally, when checking for cycles or a suspected stall","Cheap most of the time, but recovery after a real deadlock is expensive"]]}

This is exactly why avoidance carries real, ongoing runtime cost compared to prevention: prevention pays its price once at design time, while avoidance pays a little on every allocation decision for as long as the system runs. Beyond the runtime cost, the algorithm's biggest practical obstacle is its core assumption, that every process can and will declare its maximum possible future need for every resource type up front, accurately, before it ever runs.

Real, dynamic workloads rarely know this in advance. A general purpose program might open a handful of files or thousands depending entirely on user input, request more memory as it processes data, or spawn threads on demand. Declaring an accurate hard ceiling ahead of time is often either impossible or forces such a pessimistically large number that it defeats the purpose of tracking it at all. Because of this, production kernels overwhelmingly favor cheaper strategies such as careful lock ordering, timeouts, or simply accepting a small residual risk and relying on detection and recovery instead. The Banker approach survives mainly in specialized fixed resource systems, such as embedded controllers with a small known pool, or as a component inside database engines allocating fixed resource pools, and, above all, in courses and interviews.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785408759064-15559559.png
blocks.alt: Complexity, and Why Avoidance Is Rare in Production

blocks.content: 10. Common Mistakes and the Interview Angle
blocks.text: 10. Common Mistakes and the Interview Angle

blocks.content: A few specific errors show up again and again when people first work through this algorithm by hand, and every one of them is easy to make and easy to catch once you know to look for it.

The worked example in this chapter is designed to surface exactly these mistakes if you rerun it yourself: skip the subtraction in Need, or stop the safety scan too early, and the numbers stop matching the tables above.

["Computing Need directly from Max alone, forgetting it must be Max minus Allocation specifically. This silently overstates how much more a process might still ask for, and can make a genuinely safe state look unsafe on paper, or hide a real problem in the other direction.","Stopping the Safety Algorithm scan too early by walking through processes once, in a fixed order such as P0 through P4, and declaring the state unsafe the moment the first unfinished process in that order does not currently fit. The correct algorithm must try every remaining unfinished process at each round, not just the next one on a list, exactly as Section 6 shows P0 failing first while P1 succeeds.","Forgetting the rollback step in the Resource Request Algorithm: pretend granting a request, finding the resulting state unsafe, and then either granting it anyway or leaving Allocation, Need and Available stuck in the hypothetical state instead of restoring all three to exactly what they were before."]
items: Computing Need directly from Max alone, forgetting it must be Max minus Allocation specifically. This silently overstates how much more a process might still ask for, and can make a genuinely safe state look unsafe on paper, or hide a real problem in the other direction.

Stopping the Safety Algorithm scan too early by walking through processes once, in a fixed order such as P0 through P4, and declaring the state unsafe the moment the first unfinished process in that order does not currently fit. The correct algorithm must try every remaining unfinished process at each round, not just the next one on a list, exactly as Section 6 shows P0 failing first while P1 succeeds.

Forgetting the rollback step in the Resource Request Algorithm: pretend granting a request, finding the resulting state unsafe, and then either granting it anyway or leaving Allocation, Need and Available stuck in the hypothetical state instead of restoring all three to exactly what they were before.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.content: The Banker's Algorithm is one of the single most commonly asked deep operating systems questions in interviews and exams, precisely because it resists a one line answer. Interviewers expect you to build Allocation, Max, Need and Available for a small scenario from scratch, trace the Safety Algorithm by hand to a real safe sequence, and then evaluate one specific resource request against it end to end, exactly as this chapter just did. Practicing that full walkthrough with real numbers, not just reciting the definition, is the single best preparation there is.
